Flame graph: coloring scheme to visually distinguish kernel space and user space frames

**What would you like to be added**:

It would be nice to color the flame graph so that kernel space and user space frames are clearly distinguishable, for example via an additional color scheme option in the panel.

This would mainly be useful for profiles from sources that provide information about where a frame comes from (e.g. the executable or shared library, or the kernel), such as eBPF-based profiles ingested into Pyroscope via OTLP.

**Why is this needed**:

When analyzing CPU profiles, it's important to quickly see whether time is spent in application code or in the kernel. Right now this can only be found out by inspecting frames one by one.

**Who is this feature for?**

Users of the Flame graph panel who analyze CPU profiles and want to quickly see the split between kernel and user space time.

Tempo streaming search: list loads forever when stream data arrives before the subscribe reply

With "Streaming: search queries" enabled on a Tempo data source, the trace list in
Traces Drilldown (Traces tab) and the TraceQL search in Explore sometimes stay in the
loading state forever. No error is shown. A reload sometimes works.

Messages on `/api/live/ws` for the channel `<namespace>/ds/<uid>/search/<uuid>`,
over 13 page loads with no network errors:

- 8 loads hung. In all 8, both `push` messages arrived before the reply
  `{"id":N,"subscribe":{}}`. The table stayed on placeholder rows and the client never
  sent `unsubscribe`.
- 5 loads worked. In the ones with clean timings, the subscribe reply arrived first, then
  the pushes, then the client sent `unsubscribe`.
- The time range made no difference (30 minutes, 24 hours, 7 days).
- First push: 80 to 220 ms after the subscribe. Subscribe reply: 50 ms to 1.5 s after it.

On play.grafana.org, same build, 4 of 4 loads worked. There the subscribe reply came
110 to 220 ms after the subscribe and the first push 400 to 650 ms after it.

My reading: publications that arrive before the subscribe reply are dropped by the
client, and the stream has already finished, so nothing else arrives. I have not
confirmed this in the code.

Possibly related: grafana/traces-drilldown#475 and grafana/traces-drilldown#157 describe
the same symptom and were closed without a root cause.

The list loads whatever the order of the two messages.

Not sure. It hung now and then a few weeks ago as well, but much less often. Since last week it has started to become unusable

1. Open Drilldown > Traces > Traces tab, last 30 minutes, no filters.
2. Reload a number of times.

The stack must hold little trace data, so that the search answers in about 100 to 200 ms.
On a busy stack the subscribe reply wins and the list loads.

Runtime: Remove the `@alpha` tag from API discovery

**Parent:** #137723 · **Depends on:** #137724, #137727, #137728, #137729

The discovery service is exported from `@grafana/runtime` tagged `@alpha`, so its shape can still change. Plugins use it through `@grafana/plugin-compat` (#137731), which absorbs such changes, but direct callers have no stability guarantee.

- Once the internal callers (MT data source fill, plugin wrappers, generated clients) and plugin-compat have used the API without breaking changes, remove the `@alpha` tag.
- Fix any rough edges found while migrating first (renames, return types), and update `@grafana/plugin-compat` in the same release if a shape changes.
- Make sure every exported function and type has TSDoc written for plugin developers: what "not served" vs. "unknown" means, that discovery isn't permission-aware, and that callers own their fallback.

Runtime: Resolve the plugin metas API version through discovery

**Parent:** #137723 · **Depends on:** #137724 · **Related:** #137728

The plugin meta cache (`packages/grafana-runtime/src/services/pluginMeta/`: `plugins.ts`, `apps.ts`, `datasources.ts`, `panels.ts`) builds `plugins.grafana.app` URLs from `getApiVersion()`, which always returns `v0alpha1`. Unlike the settings, health and proxy wrappers (#137728), the metas load on the boot path, so resolving the version through discovery adds a `GET /apis` request in series before `/metas`.

- Measure the cost first: the time to first `/metas` response with and without a discovery request, on MT dev and on ST.
- Then pick one:
  - resolve `plugins.grafana.app` through `resolveApiVersion` and prefetch discovery early enough that it's usually cached, or
  - keep the static version for the boot-time request, and switch to discovery only for later refetches (`refetchPluginMetas` after plugin changes).
- Remove `getApiVersion()` once nothing uses it.

Alerting provisioning reload returns 500 when HA replicas reload concurrently

In a Grafana HA deployment, concurrent calls to `POST /api/admin/provisioning/alerting/reload` from alert sidecars in multiple Grafana Pods cause one or more requests to return HTTP 500 due to an optimistic-lock conflict while updating an alert rule.

Concurrent reload requests should be serialized, safely deduplicated, or otherwise complete without an HTTP 500 / version-conflict error.

1. Deploy Grafana with two replicas sharing one PostgreSQL database.
2. Deploy it with the [grafana-community/helm-charts](https://github.com/grafana-community/helm-charts) Grafana chart and enable the alert sidecar on both replicas so each sidecar watches the same alerting ConfigMaps.
3. Update a ConfigMap containing a file-provisioned alerting resource.
4. Both sidecars detect the update and call `POST http://localhost:3000/api/admin/provisioning/alerting/reload` concurrently.
5. Observe an HTTP 500 from at least one reload request.

- Grafana version: `13.3.0`
- Platform: Kubernetes
- Deployment chart: [grafana-community/helm-charts](https://github.com/grafana-community/helm-charts)
- Grafana replicas: 2
- Database: CloudNativePG PostgreSQL cluster, shared by both Grafana replicas
- Connection path: Grafana → CloudNativePG PgBouncer Pooler (two replicas, read/write) → PostgreSQL
- PgBouncer version: `1.25.1`
- Pool mode: `session`
- `default_pool_size` at the time of the incident: `10`
- Alert sidecar image: `quay/kiwigrid/k8s-sidecar:2.14.1`

The pooler is included for completeness. It was saturated during surrounding traffic and caused a preceding reload request to time out, but the HTTP 500 described here was directly caused by the alert-rule version conflict.

One reload request returned HTTP 500 after 2.65 seconds while provisioning an alert rule.

Relevant error:

`version conflict while updating alert rule ... version <N>`

At the same time, both replicas had invoked the reload endpoint. A preceding sidecar request also timed out after 10 seconds and retried, which may increase the likelihood of overlapping reloads.

This appears related to https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/75877, but the distinguishing factor here is concurrent file-provisioning reloads from multiple HA replicas sharing PostgreSQL.

As an operational mitigation, restricting the reload initiator to a single replica avoids the conflict, but this removes automatic failover for reloads. It would be useful for the reload endpoint to coordinate concurrent provisioning runs across HA instances.

Signal explorer: add the metric and label along with a label or value in "Add to query"

"Add to query" in the Signal explorer currently inserts only the text of the row that was clicked. Since every label and value is listed under its metric, the explorer already knows the full selector it belongs to. So adding a label could also include its metric, and adding a value could include its metric and label.

For example, adding `bedroom` from the `room` label of `temperature_celsius` would produce `temperature_celsius{room="bedroom"}`.

With this, users could build a valid selector from the explorer in a single click, without typing the metric name, braces and matcher themselves.

SQL query editor: “Copy code and switch” discards edits when copying fails

When switching a SQL query from **Code** to **Builder**, clicking **Copy code and switch** closes the confirmation dialog and replaces the edited SQL with the Builder query even when the browser refuses to copy. Nothing reaches the clipboard, no error is shown, and the edited SQL is no longer in the editor. On failure, the action effectively behaves like **Discard code and switch**.

Switch to Builder only after the copy succeeds. If it fails, keep the edited SQL intact, show a copy error, and let the user retry, cancel, or explicitly discard the code.

Unknown. The mode switch already happens independently of clipboard success on `main`; #138568 surfaced the issue during review but did not introduce it. #138531 tracks whether the clipboard helper reports a refused copy; this issue tracks how the SQL editor handles that failure.

1. In a SQL query editor, switch from Builder to Code and edit the SQL so it differs from the Builder query.
2. Use a browser context where the clipboard write is refused. For a deterministic component test, force the legacy clipboard path and stub `document.execCommand('copy')` to return `false`.
3. Select **Builder**, then click **Copy code and switch**.
4. The dialog closes and the query is replaced with Builder SQL even though the copy failed.

Reproduced in a Jest/jsdom component test against #138568 merged with `main` (`e4701fc6926`). The test clicked the actual confirmation dialog and verified that the editor received the Builder SQL after the copy command returned `false`.

Shared SQL editor (`@grafana/sql`); reproduced with the PostgreSQL dialect. The [confirmation handler](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/e4701fc6926/packages/grafana-sql/src/components/QueryHeader.tsx#L281-L296) is shared across SQL dialects.

Time series: show the duration of the drag selection while selecting a range to zoom

**Why is this needed**:

When investigating short events in a time series panel (from a few minutes down to sub-second), I drag across the graph to select the span of interest. While dragging, the tooltip shows only the timestamp under the cursor, so to know how long the selection is I have to read its start and end and subtract them by eye. That is slow and error-prone at fine resolution (e.g. `12:06:59.871` → `12:07:01.004`) and across minute or hour boundaries.

Often the goal is to *measure* an event (how long a value held a level, how long a spike or gap lasted) rather than to zoom. Today the only way is to zoom in, read the new range in the time picker, and zoom back out. At sub-second ranges the time picker is also rounded to whole seconds (#103243), so it can't be used to read the duration either.

In the screenshot below a selection is in progress: the tooltip shows a single timestamp (`12:07:53`) and nothing tells how long the selected span is.

**What would you like to be added**:

While a drag selection is in progress, show its duration, updated live as the cursor moves, either in the tooltip or as a label attached to the selection rectangle. For example:

```
12:06:59.871 → 12:07:01.004   Δ 1s 133ms
```

- The duration uses the largest units that fit, down to milliseconds: `2h 14m`, `3m 05s`, `1s 133ms`, `250ms`.
- Start and end are shown at the precision of the axis.
- Releasing the mouse zooms exactly as it does today; this only adds information during the drag.

**Who is this feature for?**

Users of the panels with drag-to-zoom (time series, and also candlestick, heatmap, state timeline and status history) who investigate short-lived events in high-resolution data: latency spikes, incident timelines, sensor or market data. In particular anyone who uses the drag selection as a measuring tool, not only to zoom.

This was requested before in #30625 (2021). It was moved to Discussion #38209, which was closed in 2024 when feature requests moved back out of Discussions, with an invitation to open a new issue if still wanted. Related, but about the whole dashboard range rather than the drag selection: #1492 and #66066.

Alerting: state of a rule deleted right after startup (before the first scheduler tick) stays in the state cache forever

A rule deleted in the first few seconds after Grafana starts keeps its alert state in the state cache. The state is never removed while that Grafana process runs.

The stale instance:

- still shows as `Alerting` in `GET /api/prometheus/grafana/api/v1/alerts`;
- is still counted by `grafana_alerting_alerts{state="alerting"}`;
- belongs to a rule that no longer exists (`GET /api/v1/provisioning/alert-rules/{uid}` returns 404).

Grafana logs nothing when this happens.

The window is between `stateManager.Warm()` and the scheduler's first tick. The first tick lands on the next base-interval mark, so the window can be up to 10 s long.

Cause, from the v13.0.1 code:

1. At startup, `startEvaluation` calls `stateManager.Warm()` first ([evaluation_runner.go#L45](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.0.1/pkg/services/ngalert/evaluation_runner.go#L45)). It then starts the scheduler ([#L58](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.0.1/pkg/services/ngalert/evaluation_runner.go#L58)). `Warm()` loads the saved instances of every rule that exists at that moment into the cache.
2. The scheduler finds deleted rules only among rules it has already registered. See `registeredDefinitions := sch.registry.keyMap()` ([schedule.go#L299](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.0.1/pkg/services/ngalert/schedule/schedule.go#L299)) and `toDelete` ([#L421-L425](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.0.1/pkg/services/ngalert/schedule/schedule.go#L421-L425)).
3. Only the rule's own routine removes its state, when it is stopped with `errRuleDeleted` ([alert_rule.go#L384-L387](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.0.1/pkg/services/ngalert/schedule/alert_rule.go#L384-L387)).
4. A rule deleted before the first tick is never registered. So the scheduler never sees it as deleted, no routine is stopped, and `DeleteStateByRuleUID` never runs.
5. Nothing else checks cache entries against the rule table. The stale-state check (`processMissingSeriesStates`) runs only when the rule itself is evaluated. `Warm()` skips instances of missing rules only at startup ([manager.go#L190-L193](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.0.1/pkg/services/ngalert/state/manager.go#L190-L193)).

The same code is still in `main` (checked 2026-11-18).

**Possible fix:** on each tick (or at least the first tick after `Warm()`), remove cache entries whose rule UID is not in the rule set the scheduler just fetched. Use the same path as `DeleteStateByRuleUID`, so a resolved notification and a state-history entry are written.

**Related:**

- #79953 "Cleanup orphan instances by rule on startup" (closed without merging). Its description says such instances "will simply live in the cache until either a restart or a rule update occurs".
- #129504 adds an opt-in warm gate. It does not close this window by default.

When a rule is deleted, its state is removed from the cache. Timing should not matter. `grafana_alerting_alerts` and the alerts API should never report instances of a rule that does not exist.

Not known. We first saw it in v13.0.1. The startup order (Warm, then the scheduler, then deleted rules found from the registry) looks the same in earlier versions.

The steps use the provisioning API. `$G` is the Grafana URL with admin credentials. Each step that changes something sends the `X-Disable-Provenance: true` header.

1. Create a folder and a rule group with interval `10s`. Add one rule that always fires: a Prometheus query `vector(1)`, a threshold `> 0`, and `for: 0s`, with UID `repro-rule`:
   `PUT $G/api/v1/provisioning/folder/{folderUid}/rule-groups/{group}`
2. Wait until the rule is `Alerting` in `GET $G/api/prometheus/grafana/api/v1/alerts?includeInternalLabels=true`. Then wait 15 s more, so the instance is saved to the database.
3. Restart Grafana (for example `kubectl rollout restart deploy/grafana`, or `docker restart`).
4. Follow the new process's log. As soon as `msg="State cache has been initialized"` appears, delete the rule:
   `DELETE $G/api/v1/provisioning/alert-rules/repro-rule` (returns 204).
   The delete must land before the scheduler's `first_tick` shown in the log.
5. Check:
   - `GET $G/api/v1/provisioning/alert-rules/repro-rule` returns 404.
   - `GET $G/api/prometheus/grafana/api/v1/alerts?includeInternalLabels=true` still lists an `Alerting` instance with `__alert_rule_uid__="repro-rule"`.
   - `grafana_alerting_alerts{state="alerting"}` on `/metrics` still counts it.

Our run (log times in UTC):

```
09:52:13.889 logger=ngalert.state.manager msg="Warming state cache for startup"
09:52:13.930 logger=ngalert.state.manager msg="State cache has been initialized" states=89 duration=41.121408ms
09:52:13.930 logger=ngalert.scheduler msg=starting component=ticker first_tick=2026-11-18T09:52:20Z
09:52:14.035 msg="Request Completed" method=DELETE path=/api/v1/provisioning/alert-rules/repro5958-rule status=204
09:52:15.064 msg="Request Completed" method=GET  path=/api/v1/provisioning/alert-rules/repro5958-rule status=404
```

The instance stayed `Alerting`, and was counted by the gauge, for the full 150 s we watched (15 ticks).

**Control:** we created the same rule again with no restart, waited 25 s so the scheduler registered it, and deleted it. The state was gone within 10 s.

**Workarounds:**

- Restart Grafana again. `Warm()` skips instances whose rule is gone.
- Create a rule with the same UID, wait one tick, then delete it. Its new routine removes all instances for that UID, including the stale one.

Keep dashboard traffic off the active alert evaluator in single-node evaluation mode

**Why is this needed**:
We run Grafana Enterprise 13.3.1 on AWS ECS behind an Application Load Balancer, with:
[unified_alerting]
enabled = true
execute_alerts = true
ha_single_node_evaluation = true

Grafana elects one instance to evaluate all alert rules. However, that instance also receives interactive dashboard traffic from the load balancer.

Dashboard queries, rendering and editing can compete with alert evaluation for resources. We would like to isolate these workloads while preserving automatic evaluator failover.

**What would you like to be added**:
- An evaluator-aware readiness endpoint that a load balancer can use to route dashboard traffic to other instances.
- Dedicated evaluator roles that preserve alert status and alert management through user-facing Grafana instances.

Routing eligibility should update automatically when the elected evaluator changes.

A routing endpoint should distinguish eligibility for dashboard traffic from process health, so an evaluator is not restarted simply because it is excluded from user traffic.

**Expected behaviour**:
- The active evaluator continues evaluating rules and delivering notifications.
- Dashboard traffic goes to other healthy instances.
- Evaluator failover remains automatic.
- Users can view current alert status and manage rules, silences and contact points through the normal Grafana URL.
- Behaviour is defined when no separate dashboard-serving instance is available.

**Alternatives considered**:
Separate ECS services for dashboards and evaluators, with execute_alerts=false on dashboard instances and evaluator instances excluded from the ALB.
This adds operational complexity, and Grafana’s documentation notes alert-status limitations when mixing instances with alert execution enabled and disabled.

**Environment**:
- Grafana Enterprise 13.3.1
- AWS ECS/Fargate
- AWS Application Load Balancer
- Shared PostgreSQL database
- Grafana Alerting HA using Memberlist
- Single-node evaluation enabled

Dashboard transformation does not interpolate ${interface} in the “Filter fields by name” regex on Grafana 13.3.1

In Grafana 13.3.1, the Filter fields by name transformation does not appear to interpolate the interface dashboard variable when the variable is used as part of a field name in the regular expression.

The data comes from Redis using:

```
HGETALL network:traffic:current_hour
```
The returned fields include:
```
record_time
eth0:rx
eth0:tx
eth1:rx
eth1:tx
ppp0:rx
ppp0:tx
```
The dashboard variable is named interface, and its value is eth0.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Create a dashboard variable named interface with the value eth0.
2. Query the Redis hash network:traffic:current_hour.
3. Add the Filter fields by name transformation.
4. Use this regular expression:

```
^(record_time|${interface}:rx)$
```
5. Check the fields returned by the transformation.

**Expected result**

The transformation should keep both record_time and eth0:rx, because the variable should expand to eth0 and produce:

```
^(record_time|eth0:rx)$
```
**Actual result**

Only record_time is retained. The eth0:rx field is not retained.

The equivalent literal expression works correctly:

```
^(record_time|eth0:rx)$
```
The ${interface:raw} variant also does not resolve the issue:

```
^(record_time|${interface:raw}:rx)$
```
This suggests that variable interpolation may not work correctly inside the regular expression used by the **Filter fields by name** transformation, or that the transformation receives a different interpolated value than expected.

**Environment**

- Grafana version: 13.3.1
- Data source: Redis
- Dashboard variable: interface
- Variable value: eth0

Please let me know if additional dashboard JSON, query output, or debug information is needed.

CODEOWNERS: catch missing ownership for new files before pushing

Missing CODEOWNERS coverage is often discovered only after pushing a new file and waiting for CI. Local tests and lint can pass, yet the PR still needs another commit and CI cycle just to assign ownership. This applies to any newly added file that would fail the CI ownership check, not only E2E tests.

A recent example is #138519: a new dashboard time-picker accessibility E2E spec passed locally, including 10 repeated runs, but was missing an owner. We added the CODEOWNERS entry afterward. E2E is one example of the broader workflow problem.

Add a fast, local pre-commit check that catches missing ownership before changes are pushed, for both human and agent contributors.

- Check every newly added or renamed staged file against the staged `.github/CODEOWNERS` contents. Adding a file and its owner in the same commit should pass.
- Match the existing CI ownership check's scope, exclusions, pattern precedence, and requirements. If CI would reject a file for missing ownership, the local check should reject it too; do not impose a stricter blanket requirement on files CI intentionally excludes.
- Reuse the CI validation implementation or shared configuration wherever possible, rather than maintaining a separate interpretation.
- Fail with an actionable message listing affected paths and explaining where to add the responsible team.
- Keep the check fast and offline. When CODEOWNERS changes, also detect existing files that would lose required ownership.
- Keep CI validation as the backstop for commits that bypass local hooks.

Document the requirement and standalone validation command in contributor guidance and relevant agent skills. The hook should enforce the requirement; documentation should explain how to satisfy it.

Contributors learn about missing ownership locally, before pushing and waiting for CI, regardless of file type or directory. Any ownership failure that CI would report for newly added or renamed files should be caught by the pre-commit check.

Notebooks: Support in-page anchor links

**Why is this needed**:

Grafana Notebooks are frequently used for runbooks, incident post-mortems, and complex investigation documentation. As these notebooks grow in length with multiple Markdown, query, and visualization cells, navigating them becomes difficult. Currently, there is no built-in way to link directly to a specific heading or cell within the same notebook (or share a direct link to a specific section of a notebook with teammates during an active incident).

Supporting in-page anchor links would significantly improve navigation, allow authors to build a clickable Table of Contents at the top of long runbooks, and speed up incident response by letting engineers jump straight to relevant diagnostic sections.

**What would you like to be added**:

Support standard Markdown anchor links and heading IDs within Grafana Notebooks:

1. **Auto-generated heading IDs:** Automatically generate slugified anchor IDs for Markdown headings (`#`, `##`, `###`, etc.) rendered inside notebook text cells (matching standard GitHub-Flavored Markdown behavior).
2. **Smooth scrolling on click:** Clicking an internal anchor link (e.g., `[Jump to Database Latency](#database-latency)`) should smoothly scroll the notebook view to the target heading rather than attempting a full page navigation or failing to resolve.

**Who is this feature for?**

- **SREs and On-Call Engineers** who rely on lengthy Grafana Notebooks as incident runbooks and need to jump quickly between triage steps or share direct section links during outages.
- **Technical Writers and Platform Teams** who author documentation, onboarding guides, or investigation templates in Notebooks and want to include a clickable Table of Contents.

Public Dashboards: repeated panels fail with 404 panelNotFound — clone panels send djb2Hash(pathId) as panelId, which the public query API cannot resolve

When a dashboard that uses panel `repeat` is shared as a public dashboard, only the
first instance of each repeat group renders data. Every subsequent clone fails with
`publicdashboards.panelNotFound`:

POST /api/public/dashboards/<accessToken>/panels/2699174418/query → 404
{"statusCode":404,"messageId":"publicdashboards.panelNotFound","message":"Dashboard panel not found ..."}

Panel titles render correctly (client-side scoped variables), so the failure only
shows up as missing data / error state on clones 2..N. The first clone of each group
works, which makes the bug look partial/intermittent.

Root cause (verified against v13.3.1 and main):

- `DashboardScene.enrichDataRequest`
  (public/app/features/dashboard-scene/scene/DashboardScene.tsx):

    if (isRepeatCloneOrChildOf(panel)) {
      // can't use the original panel ID in this case
      panelId = djb2Hash(panel.getPathId());
    } else {
      panelId = getPanelIdForVizPanel(panel);
    }

  On the normal /api/ds/query path this is fine — panelId is only used as request
  metadata. But the public-dashboard query handler
  (packages/grafana-runtime/src/utils/publicDashboardQueryHandler.ts) forwards that
  panelId to POST /api/public/dashboards/{accessToken}/panels/{panelId}/query.

- The public dashboard backend
  (pkg/services/publicdashboards/internal/service/query.go,
  groupQueriesByPanelId / extractQueriesFromPanels) indexes the saved dashboard's
  panels by their real saved IDs only. A djb2 hash of the clone's path ID
  (<repeatValue>$panel-<sourceId>) has no match → ErrPanelNotFound.

- The first clone of each repeat group reuses the original VizPanel object
  (index === 0 ? panelToRepeat : panelToRepeat.clone(...) in DashboardGridItem),
  so it has no repeatSourceKey, sends the real panel ID, and succeeds.

Measured confirmation: for a panel with `repeat` over a custom variable, the failing
POST IDs in the browser console are exactly djb2Hash("<value>$panel-<sourcePanelId>"),
e.g. djb2Hash("CNAF-DATA-SE$panel-3456") = 2699174418.

What did you expect to happen?

All repeated instances of a panel should render data on the public dashboard — e.g.
by the frontend sending the repeat-source panel ID for clones (public dashboards only
execute the stored queries, so clones of the same source share the same stored query),
or the backend resolving the clone path ID back to its source panel.

Did this work before?

No. Public dashboards only execute the queries stored on the dashboard, and the docs
list template variables as a limitation — repeat-driven per-instance queries were
never part of that contract.

How do we reproduce it?

1. Create a dashboard with a panel backed by a backend datasource, set `Repeat by`
   to a variable with ≥ 2 values.
2. Share → Public dashboard → open the public URL.
3. First repeated instance renders data; instances 2..N show "Dashboard panel not
   found" (devtools: POST /api/public/dashboards/<uid>/panels/<large-integer>/query → 404).
4. Direct API check: POST /api/public/dashboards/<uid>/panels/<sourceId>/query → 200;
   the hashed clone ID → 404.

MCP Apps need a time range picker without the backward, forward, and zoom buttons for now. The existing `TimeRangePicker` combines those toolbar controls with the range selection UI, while `TimePickerContent` already provides the selection UI separately.

Notebooks already uses `TimePickerContent`, but [reaches into `packages/grafana-ui/src` through a relative import in `NotebookCellTimeRangeControl.tsx`](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/8c78f7884e076368311323cfb691b08271595698/public/app/features/notebook/scene/layout-notebook/edit/NotebookCellTimeRangeControl.tsx#L30). It also deep-imports `getQuickOptions`. This leaves consumers coupled to private implementation paths.

Expose the standalone selection UI from `@grafana/ui/unstable` under a clearer name, provisionally `TimeRangeSelector`, together with `TimeRangeSelectorProps`.

- Reuse the existing range selection implementation, including relative and absolute ranges and the existing timezone/history options.
- Supply standard quick ranges by default, while allowing callers to override them. Consumers should not need to import `getQuickOptions` from a private path.
- Keep the trigger, popover lifecycle, navigation/zoom controls, and history persistence in the consuming shell.

The MCP renderer bundles its own version of `@grafana/ui`. Pinning that dependency allows API changes to be handled as coordinated renderer upgrades rather than depending on the host Grafana version. We accept the need to update these consumers when the unstable API changes; this does not introduce a stable compatibility guarantee.

Grafana 14 could be a point to revisit the API, migrate consumers, or promote the component to a stable export. That is a possible checkpoint, not a requirement to retain the unstable API unchanged until then.

- A named standalone range selector and its props are available from `@grafana/ui/unstable`.
- Default quick ranges work without private imports; custom quick ranges remain supported.
- Notebooks uses the package export with equivalent selection, history, and dismissal behavior.
- The MCP App picker supports range selection without backward, forward, or zoom buttons.
- Existing full-picker consumers retain their current behavior.

Text v2: Deprecate fmt in favor of display and add template migration

Follow-up to #137542 (merged November 20, 2026) and #136478. Parent epic: #128614.

Deprecate the Text v2 `fmt` namespace in favor of the `display` helper, including `{{#display "cpu"}}...{{/display}}` for access to formatted text, units, mappings, and colors. Add migration assistance in the Text panel for existing templates.

Code review of `v2/handlebars.ts`, its existing tests, `suggestions.ts`, and `v2/textPanelMigrationHandler.ts` indicates a conservative migration is feasible, but a blanket replacement is not semantics-preserving. This is a static assessment, not a tested migration implementation.

- Direct reads can use `{{fmt.cpu}}` → `{{display "cpu"}}`; helper arguments can use `fmt.cpu` → `(display "cpu")`. Explicit row paths can use `{{data.[0].fmt.cpu}}` → `{{display "cpu" row=data.[0]}}` when the row context is established.
- Prefer the inline helper for automatic string-preserving rewrites. The block form changes context and yields a display object; it cannot replace string-valued arguments or conditions directly. For manual block conversion, `{{#display "cpu"}}{{this}}{{/display}}` prints the complete formatted value; `{{text}}` alone loses unit prefix/suffix.
- The helper resolves rows through a WeakMap keyed by original row identity. Inline partials with hash arguments copy their context; these require an explicit original `row=` reference. A mechanical rewrite there can silently produce empty output.
- `#each fmt`, `#with fmt`, dynamic `lookup`, aliases/parent paths, and a real field named `fmt` need contextual analysis or manual handling. Existing tests explicitly support these patterns, including a field shadowing the namespace. The saved panel migration handler receives options, not query field metadata, so it cannot reliably disambiguate every occurrence.
- Parse templates and rewrite verified expressions using source locations; do not use regex substitution. Preserve bracketed/quoted field names, whitespace controls, double/triple-brace escaping, comments, and unrelated content. Scope conversion to content actually interpreted as Handlebars; Code mode and literal/protected content must remain intact.

Implementation entry point: `public/app/plugins/panel/text/v2/textPanelMigrationHandler.ts` already handles legacy options, but a safe template converter and editor assistance need new implementation. Existing `handlebars.test.ts` parity cases provide a useful regression corpus.

Table: Research field identity and display-name semantics for ad-hoc transformations

Part of grafana/grafana-org#1023.

Investigate how field identity and display names should work across table interactions, transformations, field overrides, saved configuration, and URL state.

Renaming a column through a Display name override should behave as consistently as possible with renaming it through Organize fields. Currently, Organize renames happen within the transformation pipeline, while field overrides apply afterward. Both use display-name configuration, but transformations cannot see names introduced by later overrides.

#138302 fixes hide/reorder controls by translating between the names the table displays and the names the Organize transformation matches. This addresses the immediate bug, but leaves a broader design question: can we establish a shared field-reference model instead of adding translation and special cases for each operation?

- URL sync (#136215) will serialize field references. We should settle their semantics before the URL format becomes a compatibility commitment, or explicitly plan versioning and migration.
- More ad-hoc transformations, including sorting, grouping, and pivoting, will increase the amount of name translation and special-case code we may later need to replace.

- Compare making Display name overrides behave more like Organize renames with separating field identity from display labels. Do not assume moving overrides earlier is safe: transformations can create fields that overrides must target.
- Define how references behave across renames, duplicate source/display names, multiple frames, changing query results, and transformations that create, remove, or reshape fields.
- Identify a shared approach for table controls, transformation matching, saved dashboard configuration, and URL serialization/restoration.
- Assess compatibility with existing dashboards and the current ad-hoc transformation layer (#133138), including whether an incremental approach can replace existing translation logic.

A documented recommendation with tradeoffs, examples, compatibility requirements, and scoped implementation follow-ups. Resolve the field-reference decision before finalizing #136215's serialization format. This research does not require delaying the immediate bug fix in #138302.

Apply ad-hoc operations to a field, then change its display name through the upstream Organize fields transformation. The existing ad-hoc state should still target the same logical field: hiding, ordering, filtering, and other supported operations should not be lost or redirected to another field. Cover both the live state and restoration from saved/URL state where supported. This is distinct from changing a Display name field override, because an Organize rename changes the names downstream transformations see.

This may require research down to the DataFrame/Field model, rather than only table-level name mapping. Investigate whether field identity or lineage can survive transformations, and define what happens when operations create, merge, split, or replace fields. Stable identity across those operations is a hard design problem; the research should establish the limits and compatibility implications before choosing an implementation.

Database: locking_attempt_timeout_sec is ignored on PostgreSQL, concurrent instances fail with "failed to obtain lock"

When several Grafana instances start at the same time against the same PostgreSQL database, only one of them gets the migration lock. The others exit immediately with `failed to obtain lock`, even with `locking_attempt_timeout_sec = 60`:

```
logger=migrator t=2026-11-19T14:39:50.690356398Z level=info msg="Locking database"
logger=migrator t=2026-11-19T14:39:50.691192716Z level=error msg="Failed to lock database" error="failed to obtain lock"
Error: ✗ failed to obtain lock
```

The error comes less than 1 ms after `Locking database`, so the timeout is not applied. `PostgresDialect.Lock()` runs `SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(?)`, which returns at once, and never reads `cfg.Timeout`:
https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.3.1/pkg/services/sqlstore/migrator/postgres_dialect.go#L299-L317

The MySQL dialect passes the timeout (`SELECT GET_LOCK(?, ?)`):
https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.3.1/pkg/services/sqlstore/migrator/mysql_dialect.go#L280

`conf/defaults.ini` documents the setting for both:
https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/v13.3.1/conf/defaults.ini#L295-L296

It also happens when the database is already migrated (the lock is taken on every start), and in the secret migrator, which with Grafana 13.3.1 on PostgreSQL also fails with `running secret database migrations: failed to obtain lock` (see below).

We hit it on Kubernetes (2 replicas): on the first install one pod crashes and restarts once.

Related:
- #135481 / #135551: same problem in the secret migrator, reported on MySQL. The fix relies on the timeout, so it has no effect on PostgreSQL.
- With MySQL, once the lock waits, instances can still exit later in the same test with `there is already a lock for this actionName: oss-ac-basic-role-seeder` (the second error in #135481), so fixing the PostgreSQL lock alone may not be enough for concurrent starts.

With `locking_attempt_timeout_sec` > 0, instances that lose the race wait for the lock, as they do on MySQL.

Text: Research Pele as the Text v2 diagram rendering engine

Evaluate [Pele](https://pele.run/) as a replacement for Text v2's Mermaid diagram renderer. This would replace only diagram rendering, not Markdown, HTML, Handlebars, or the sandbox pipeline.

Initial recommendation: prototype behind a feature flag before changing the default. The potential benefits are smaller renderer payloads, faster diagram updates, and better theme integration. The main adoption risk is visual and configuration compatibility.

The inspected Text v2 implementation uses Mermaid 11.17.2. `public/app/plugins/panel/text/v2/sandboxMermaid.ts` renders diagrams with strict security and HTML labels disabled, then sanitizes SVG with DOMPurify.

`loadSandboxRuntime.ts` loads the renderer on demand as bundled JavaScript text. The parent caches that source and sends it into the sandbox iframe. Separate iframe contexts still execute the renderer independently. Ordinary Text panels without diagrams already avoid this download.

Grafana theme settings currently come from `public/app/core/utils/mermaidConfig.ts`.

| Area | Potential benefit | Qualification or risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bundle size | Pele advertises 230 kB gzip versus 1.6 MB for Mermaid, with zero direct dependencies. | These are publisher figures, not measurements of Grafana's production bundle. Savings mainly affect the first diagram load. Other Grafana consumers may still require Mermaid. |
| Performance | Published render times are 0.05–0.3 ms versus 6–82 ms for Mermaid. Smaller code may also reduce parsing and iframe initialization costs. | These are not Grafana benchmarks. Sanitization, SVG insertion, messaging, browser layout, and paint still contribute to total latency. |
| Theming | CSS variables map naturally to Grafana tokens. Colors can change without regenerating diagrams. | Mermaid theme settings must be translated. The existing sandbox update path would need adjustment to realize theme-only savings. |
| Responsive diagrams | Layout can adapt to narrow panels instead of only scaling down. Built-in zoom is available. | Automatic direction changes and new diagram heights can affect fit-content, pagination, repeated rows, and dashboard resizing. |
| Compatibility | Pele claims all built-in Mermaid 12.1.0 diagram types. Existing Mermaid source remains usable. | Its layout engine produces different node positions, spacing, and edges. Configuration support varies; Mermaid themes do not carry over. |
| Maintenance | MIT license, developed for Obsidian, fewer dependencies. | Evaluate release stability, issue responsiveness, and the cost of following a second implementation of Mermaid syntax. |

The size and speed figures above are claims from [Pele's website](https://pele.run/), not independently verified results.

- External Mermaid plugins are unsupported.
- Arbitrary HTML labels are unsupported and JavaScript callbacks are ignored. These are limited losses for the current strict, SVG-label implementation.
- Math requires a separate resolver; custom icons may need a trusted resolver. Test existing math-heavy and icon-heavy diagrams explicitly.
- Responsive layouts can change source direction, such as switching a wide `LR` flowchart to vertical. Preserve source direction initially and evaluate adaptation separately.
- `render()` fits the existing adapter. `mount()` adds resizing and zoom but requires lifecycle cleanup and integration with panel sizing.
- Pele offers per-type and lazy imports. These must work with Grafana's controlled iframe loading; start with the complete bundle and measure before adding splitting complexity.
- Use unique SVG ID prefixes for multiple diagrams.

See [compatibility](https://pele.run/compatibility) and [API documentation](https://pele.run/api).

Retain the existing sandbox, CSP, external-resource consent, and DOMPurify sanitization. Pele's URL filtering and resource limits are additional protections, not replacements for Text v2's boundaries.

Images can make network requests. Icon and math resolvers return trusted markup. Keep render options under application control. Rendering is synchronous; a hard execution timeout would require a terminable worker.

See [Pele security documentation](https://pele.run/security) and `public/app/plugins/panel/text/v2/SANDBOX.md`.

No Grafana benchmark or implementation change has been performed as part of this initial research.

[New Data Source]: <name-of-service>

Firebird is a mature, open-source relational database widely used as the backbone for legacy and mid-market ERP, point-of-sale (POS), logistics, and manufacturing systems—especially across Latin America and Europe. Despite its large installed base in operational environments, organizations running Firebird face a significant barrier when adopting Grafana for observability and business intelligence.

Currently, there is no official or actively maintained native Firebird data source plugin. As a result, data engineers and analysts have to build and maintain redundant ETL pipelines (replicating data into PostgreSQL or MySQL) or develop custom middleware APIs just to run basic SQL queries and visualize operational metrics in Grafana.

In a commercial and supply chain operation running a Firebird-backed ERP, we need to monitor real-time operational and business KPIs on Grafana dashboards—such as daily sales performance, commercial pipeline conversion, inventory turnover, and accounts aging.

Current workaround & pain points:

    We have to run scheduled Python/ETL jobs to extract data from Firebird and load it into a secondary MySQL/PostgreSQL database solely so Grafana can query it.

    This introduces unnecessary infrastructure overhead, data latency (preventing true real-time monitoring), and extra points of failure when schemas change.

How a native Firebird connector solves this:

    Direct SQL Querying: Allows connecting directly to Firebird (versions 2.5, 3.0, 4.0, and 5.0) using standard credentials (host, port, database path/alias, user, password) with a built-in SQL query editor supporting Time Series and Table formats.

    Zero-ETL Architecture: Eliminates intermediate replication databases for small-to-medium workloads, enabling immediate, real-time operational dashboards directly from the ERP source.

    Proven Technical Feasibility: Mature Go drivers for Firebird (such as nakagami/firebirdsql) already exist, making it straightforward to implement as a standard backend SQL data source plugin alongside PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MSSQL.

Alerting: alertingSaveStatePeriodic shutdown sync can overwrite state with a partial snapshot

With `alertingSaveStatePeriodic` enabled, a graceful shutdown can write a partial snapshot of alert state to the database. That partial snapshot replaces all saved state, so the state of some rules is deleted.

On shutdown, the scheduler and the state manager stop on the same context (`evaluationRunner.startEvaluation`, `pkg/services/ngalert/evaluation_runner.go`). Two things then run at the same time:

- Each rule routine sees `grafanaCtx.Done()` and calls `stateManager.ForgetStateByRuleUID`, which removes the rule from the state cache (`pkg/services/ngalert/schedule/alert_rule.go`).
- `AsyncStatePersister.Async` sees `ctx.Done()` and runs a final `fullSync` that reads the same cache (`pkg/services/ngalert/state/persister_async.go`).

Nothing orders the two. If the final sync reads the cache after only some rule routines have cleared their entries, `ProtoInstanceDBStore.FullSync` runs `DELETE FROM alert_rule_state` and then inserts only the rules still in the cache (`pkg/services/ngalert/store/proto_instance_database.go`). The saved state of every rule cleared before the read is gone. An instance that starts next and runs `Manager.Warm` restores those rules from scratch, so their pending timers start over.

If the cache is already empty, `FullSync` returns early, which protects the "everything cleared" case but not the partial one.

The final sync on shutdown should write the complete state as it was before shutdown cleanup, or skip writing. For example:
- run the final sync before the rule routines are cancelled, or
- have the rule routines skip `ForgetStateByRuleUID` on shutdown, or
- skip the final sync once cleanup has started.

With `alertingSaveStatePeriodic` disabled, state is saved after each evaluation, and shutdown only clears the in-memory cache. No database rows are deleted on shutdown.

This is a race, found by reading the code. We have not reproduced it deterministically. Steps that should show it:

1. Enable `alertingSaveStatePeriodic` with the compressed state store (`alert_rule_state` table) and many rules. We run ~16k rules.
2. Let some rules reach Pending or Alerting.
3. Stop Grafana gracefully (SIGTERM).
4. Before any other instance writes state, compare `alert_rule_state` with the rules that had state before shutdown. Some can be missing.
5. Start an instance. Rules missing from the table start again from Normal.

- `FullSync` accepts `batchSize` and `jitterFunc` but does not use them. It deletes and rewrites the whole table in one transaction, so `state_periodic_save_batch_size` and `state_periodic_save_jitter_enabled` have no effect with this store.
- In HA without single-node evaluation, every instance runs this full-table rewrite every interval. On PostgreSQL the instances queue on row locks. In our setup, 3 instances and ~16k rules on Aurora PostgreSQL 14 spend a steady ~1.45 average active sessions on `DELETE FROM alert_rule_state`. Per-rule `DELETE ... WHERE rule_uid` statements wait behind those rewrites, with bursts of 10+ sessions in `Lock:tuple` / `Lock:transactionid`.

Table should let developers scroll to the top or bottom of the table from code, the same way the logs panel does. Two uses:

Datasource API: GET /querytypes returns 500 "namespace mismatch" for signed-in users

`GET /apis/{pluginId}.datasource.grafana.app/v0alpha1/querytypes` returns HTTP 500 for a signed-in user. The same happens for `querytypes/{name}`. Every datasource that registers query types fails this way, testdata included.

```
Internal Server Error: "/apis/grafana-testdata-datasource.datasource.grafana.app/v0alpha1/querytypes": namespace mismatch: got default but expected
```

1. Enable the feature toggles `datasource.useNewCRUDAPIs` and `datasources.queryTypes`.
2. Sign in as an admin user.
3. Request `/apis/grafana-testdata-datasource.datasource.grafana.app/v0alpha1/querytypes`.

Seen on a local build of `main` at `11cba74e935` (13.4.0).

The request returns the `QueryTypeDefinitionList`, or a 403 if the user is not allowed to read it. It must not return a 500.

Clients such as MCP servers and LLM agents need the query type schema to build valid queries. Today the OpenAPI document is the only route that returns it.

Cause

`querytypes` is cluster-scoped, so the request has no namespace. The authorizer in `pkg/registry/apis/datasource/authorizer.go` checks every resource request as a `datasources` permission and passes `Namespace: attr.GetNamespace()`, which is empty here.

The access client rejects an empty request namespace unless the namespace of the caller is `*`. A normal user has `default`, so the check returns `namespace mismatch`. The authorizer returns that error, and the API server reports a 500.

This likely started with #125513, which moved the authorizer to the authlib client. I read that diff but did not run the older code.

Possible fix: handle `attr.GetResource() == "querytypes"` in the authorizer before the namespaced check.

Frontend: Separate foundational global styles from feature-specific styles

`packages/grafana-ui/src/themes/GlobalStyles/GlobalStyles.tsx` combines foundational typography, fonts, element resets, accessibility and Markdown styles with feature-specific styles for alerting, query editors, dashboard layout, page layout and other domains.

This makes it difficult for isolated content renderers to reuse Grafana's foundational styles without also loading unrelated application CSS. Text v2 currently collects Emotion global styles into each iframe; this surfaced while investigating dashboards with many Text panels in #138087. Parent-side caching cannot eliminate CSS processing inside each frame.

- Identify a reusable foundational stylesheet with explicit ownership and a clear contract.
- Move domain-specific styles into their owning feature/component roots, using scoped selectors where possible.
- Give isolated content renderers an explicit way to consume foundational styles instead of discovering every Emotion global stylesheet.
- Preserve cascade order and audit compatibility, including legacy Text HTML that relies on global utility classes, plugins, themes and embedded content.

Moving feature styles into feature-local Emotion `Global` components alone is insufficient: the selectors remain global, and mounted features could still be collected by consumers that scan global stylesheets.

Track the application-wide ownership cleanup separately from Text-specific performance fixes. Compare typography, Markdown, code, forms and utility classes in light and dark themes; exercise affected feature screens and legacy HTML consumers. Measure stylesheet size and rendering cost before claiming a performance improvement.

The profiling in #138087 motivates this investigation but does not establish that domain CSS accounts for all remaining frame initialization cost.

list Redis-compatible servers (Valkey, KiviDB) for [remote_cache], with measured numbers

**What would you like to be added?**

A short note in the `[remote_cache]` docs saying that Redis-protocol servers other than Redis work, such as Valkey and KiviDB, and what they change for large installs.

**Why is this needed?**

With `type = redis`, OAuth token sync and ID forwarding read the remote cache on every request, from every Grafana replica. The cache layer only issues `GET`, `SET EX` and `DEL` (`pkg/infra/remotecache/redis_storage.go`), so any Redis-compatible server works unchanged.

We replayed that mix (95% `GET`, 4% `SET EX 600`, 1% `DEL`, 1.5 KB values, 10k entries) on three servers. Each server got 4 dedicated cores, and memtier ran on 4 other cores.

| Connections | Redis 8.10 | Valkey 8.1 (`--io-threads 4`) | KiviDB 1.2.2 (`--threads 4`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 48 | 116k ops/s | 290k | 316k |
| 500 | 126k | 312k | 373k |

- **p99 latency at 500 connections:** 4.7 ms on Redis, 2.2 ms on Valkey, 2.9 ms on KiviDB.
- **Memory for the dataset:** 302 MB on Redis, 299 MB on Valkey, 247 MB on KiviDB.

To try it, run one worker thread per core: `docker run -d -p 6379:6380 kividb/kividb:v1.2.2 --threads <cores> --requirepass <pw>`. Today's default uses half the cores, and a fix for that is in progress.

KiviDB is an open-source (AGPLv3), multi-threaded Redis-protocol server written in Rust. The full harness is available on request. Happy to send a docs PR if you'd like one.

CodeMirror: Editor breaks when a signature help provider throws

`signatureHelp(provider)` in `packages/grafana-ui/src/components/CodeMirror/signatureHelp.ts` calls the provider from a CodeMirror `StateField`'s `create` and `update` without catching errors. CodeMirror doesn't catch errors thrown from a state field, so a provider that throws:

- in `update`, makes every edit fail, and the user can't type in the editor.
- in `create`, makes the editor fail to load.

This already affects `main` (SQL Expressions uses `signatureHelp`). #137515 makes `signatureHelp` a public `CodeMirrorEditor` prop, so plugin code will run in this path too. It should be fixed before the API is marked stable in #136080.

**Fix**

- Catch errors from the provider, show no tooltip, and report the error with Faro, the way `useLanguageExtension.ts` reports language load failures.
- Add a test that a throwing provider doesn't break `EditorState.create` or an edit.

Once `table.refresh` is on for everyone, remove the toggle gate from the table cell inspector so its code view is always CodeMirror. Do this a few weeks after #137940 lands, once the CodeMirror view has run in rollout without problems.

* Leave the `table.refresh` flag definition to the table refresh rollout. This only removes the cell inspector's use of it.

Follow-up to #137133 and #137940, which put the CodeMirror code view behind `table.refresh`.

Add an optional copy-to-clipboard overlay to CodeMirrorEditor

Consumers displaying read-only code often need a copy-to-clipboard action. They currently render a separate `ClipboardButton` outside `CodeMirrorEditor`.

In the table cell inspector from #137940, that button occupies its own row above the editor, adds vertical spacing, and looks disconnected from the code surface.

Add an optional copy-to-clipboard overlay to the shared `CodeMirrorEditor` component. Consumers could enable a compact icon button positioned in the top-right corner of the editor without affecting document layout.

The shared implementation should use Grafana clipboard utilities and standard UI components instead of requiring each consumer to recreate positioning, accessibility, and success or error feedback.

- `CodeMirrorEditor` exposes an opt-in copy-to-clipboard control.
- Control overlays editor without changing editor height or surrounding layout.
- Control has accessible name and keyboard support.
- Copy action copies full editor contents, independent of current selection.
- User receives standard success or failure feedback.
- Control works with read-only editors and remains absent by default.

Allow read-only CodeMirrorEditor consumers to omit onChange

`CodeMirrorEditorProps` currently requires an `onChange` callback even when the editor is read-only. Read-only consumers must pass an empty callback such as:

```
<CodeMirrorEditor
  value={text}
  onChange={() => {}}
  readOnly
/>
```

This is visible in #137940. The callback has no meaningful behavior because user edits are blocked, and the empty function makes the consumer API noisier.

Allow `onChange` to be omitted for read-only editors. Possible implementations include making the callback optional for all consumers or modeling editable and read-only props as a discriminated union.

- Read-only `CodeMirrorEditor` consumers can omit `onChange`.
- Editable consumers still receive type safety requiring or otherwise correctly handling change callbacks.
- Existing editor behavior remains unchanged.
- Add coverage for a read-only editor without `onChange`.

Alerting: Alert list Time (asc/desc) sorts instances incorrectly in Custom grouping

What happened?

The Grafana Alert list panel does not correctly sort individual alert instances chronologically when using Custom grouping with Time (asc) or Time (desc).The sorting direction changes when switching between ascending and descending, but the order does not match the timestamps displayed in the Created column.This affects our NOC monitoring dashboard, where all active alert instances must be displayed individually, with the newest firing alerts at the top.

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open a dashboard containing an Alert list panel with multiple firing alert instances.
  2. Edit the panel.
  3. Select Custom grouping.
  4. Leave Group by empty so individual alert instances are displayed.
  5. Set Sort order to Time (desc).
  6. Compare the alert ordering with the displayed Created timestamps.
  7. Change the sort order to Time (asc) and observe the results.

Actual result

With Time (desc), the following ordering was observed: Alert | Created timestamp -- | -- VMWARE_ESXI_HOST_CONNECTION | 2026-11-11 15:35:40 KUBERNETES_MEMORY_UTILIZATION | 2026-11-12 16:23:40 SWAP MEMORY | 2026-11-12 12:09:20 EXPORTER_DOWN | 2026-11-12 11:58:50 An older alert from November 11 appears before newer alerts from November 12.With Time (asc), the ordering reverses, but it still does not correspond to chronological order.

Expected result

  • Time (desc): Newest active alert instance first.
  • Time (asc): Oldest active alert instance first.
  • Sorting should work correctly while retaining Custom grouping and displaying each individual alert instance separately.
  • All existing alert labels should remain visible.

Technical investigation

Environment:
  • Grafana OSS 13.2.2
  • RPM installation on RHEL 9
  • Visualization: Alert list
  • Group mode: Custom grouping
  • Group by: Empty
  • Alert state: Firing
Investigation of the installed Grafana frontend identified the following sorting logic in the compiled bundle:6540.acf453ee99146ad315f3.jsThe relevant logic uses:
sortBy(alerts, alert => [
  new Date(alert.activeAt) || new Date(),
  alertInstanceKey(alert).toLocaleLowerCase()
]).reverse()
Suspected root cause:The sorting callback returns an array containing a JavaScript Date object and a label key, rather than using separate sort iteratees with a numeric timestamp.This may cause the date value to be compared using its string representation rather than chronological ordering.A possible correction would be to use separate sort keys:
sortBy(alerts, [
  alert => new Date(alert.activeAt).getTime(),
  alert => alertInstanceKey(alert).toLocaleLowerCase()
]).reverse()
The corresponding ascending sort should use the same numeric timestamp approach without reversing.This is a suspected cause based on the frontend code and observed behavior, not a fully validated patch.

Impact

This is important for NOC operations because newly firing incidents must appear at the top of the dashboard.Default grouping is not a suitable workaround because it groups alert instances by rule and requires additional expansion to inspect individual alerts.We need to retain the Custom grouping layout while ensuring correct chronological sorting.

Units: `clocks`/`clockms` drop negative values and `isValidGoDuration` rejects `1h30m` / accepts `abc5s`

**1. `clocks` and `clockms` units drop negative values**

In `packages/grafana-data/src/valueFormats/dateTimeFormatters.ts`, `toClock` branches on `size < 1000`, `size < 60000`, `size < 3600000` without handling `size < 0` first (unlike `toDuration`, `toDurationInHoursMinutesSeconds`, and `toDurationInDaysHoursMinutesSeconds`). Any negative value takes the `size < 1000` branch and is formatted as a UTC timestamp before the epoch (`toUtc(size).format('SSS\\m\\s')`), losing both the sign and the magnitude:

- `clocks` on `-3600` (seconds) returns `'000ms'`
- `clocks` on `-65` (seconds) returns `'000ms'`
- `clockms` on `-500` (milliseconds) returns `'500ms'`

**2. `isValidGoDuration` does not match Go's `time.ParseDuration`**

In `packages/grafana-data/src/datetime/durationutil.ts`, `isValidGoDuration` documents that it checks whether a string can be parsed by Go's `time.ParseDuration`. However, `validateDurationByUnits` splits on spaces and tests each token with the unanchored regex `/([0-9]*[.]?[0-9]+)(.+)/`:

- Valid Go multi-unit durations without spaces are rejected: `isValidGoDuration('1h30m')` and `isValidGoDuration('1m30.5s')` return `false`.
- Strings with arbitrary prefixes or negative signs are accepted because the regex is not anchored: `isValidGoDuration('abc5s')` returns `true`, and `isValidGoDuration('-4.0m')` returns `true` (note that `durationutil.test.ts` includes `-4.0m` in `'3.h -4.0m 0.s 2.ms -0.us 5.ns'`, which only fails because of `3.h`).
- `10μs` (U+03BC Greek small letter mu, accepted by Go's `time.ParseDuration` alongside U+00B5 `µ`) returns `false`.

(`isValidGrafanaDuration` calls the same `validateDurationByUnits` helper and has the same behavior.)

1. Negative values formatted with `clocks` and `clockms` should preserve their magnitude and indicate that the value is negative (for example with a leading `-` or an `ago` suffix like `dthms`/`dtdhms`).
2. `isValidGoDuration` should accept standard Go duration strings such as `'1h30m'`, `'1m30.5s'`, and `'10μs'`, and reject invalid prefixes such as `'abc5s'`.

CI: Levitate check reports false breaking changes on fork PRs when `main` moves before the run is approved

The "Detect breaking changes between PR and base" job fails on fork PRs that don't change any exported API. The PR build and the base build come from different versions of `main`.

**Example 1: #136935.** This PR adds two option descriptions in `grafana-ui` and doesn't change any exports.

- **02:36 UTC Nov 12:** I pushed. GitHub created merge commit `ad16c57d5b` on top of `main` at `1bc40fb45d4`.
- **16:18 UTC:** A maintainer approved the run, and the jobs started.
- **In between:** `main` merged #137629, which added `loadCodeMirrorSetup` to `@grafana/ui/internal` (108c991), and #136737, which added var-mapping helpers to `@grafana/data`.
- **Result:** The PR build came from `ad16c57d5b`, which doesn't have those commits. The base build came from `main` at 16:18, which does. Levitate saw the new exports as exports the PR removed, and failed the check.

**Example 2: #137130 (later merged).** Its run compared a merge commit built on `main` from Nov 5 (`05d979e3398`) against `main` from Nov 11 (`9d30d3d48b3`). That's 306 commits apart, and 8 of them added exports, such as `callAppPluginProxy` in `@grafana/runtime` (#137300) and `usePanelChromeHeaderControls` in `@grafana/ui/internal` (#135056). The PR itself only changed four files in `grafana-ui/src/components/Table/`.

The PR side checks out the merge commit from the time of the push. The base side checks out the branch by name, so it gets `main` at the time the job runs:

```
# .github/workflows/detect-breaking-changes-levitate.yml
path: './base'
ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.ref }}
```

PRs from branches in this repo run right away, so the gap is usually minutes. Fork PRs wait for approval, often for hours, so they're much more likely to hit this. Re-running the job doesn't help either: it reuses the old merge commit while `main` keeps moving.

Build the base from the same commit the merge commit was built on. Either:

- check out `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` instead of `base.ref`, or
- check out the first parent of the PR merge commit (`HEAD^1` in the `./pr` checkout), which is guaranteed to match.

The second is the more robust option. I'm happy to open a PR for whichever you prefer.

`base.ref` was introduced in #45005 so backport PRs compare against their release branch. Both options above keep that behavior, because they resolve to a commit on the PR's base branch.

In the last four weeks, at least 12 fork PRs failed this check after a delay of 3 to 185 hours between the run being created and starting. 11 of them don't change any package entry point, and 9 merged with the check still failing, including #137130, #136862, #136960 and #135980.

Fork contributors get a red check with no change to fix. For forks, the details only appear in the job summary, so it isn't obvious that the failure has nothing to do with their PR. The circular-dependency check in `frontend-lint.yml` has a similar problem: its base side also checks out current `main`, and #136809 failed it with cycles that `main` had already removed.

Plugins: Expose API discovery in `@grafana/plugin-compat`

**Parent:** #137723 · **Depends on:** #137724 (group level), #138734 (`isApiResourceAvailable`)

Plugins want to ask which `/apis` groups and versions are served, and call them with their own clients. They need to do it in a way that:

- **doesn't change** when the runtime API changes or loses its `@alpha` tag, and
- **keeps working on older Grafana versions** that don't have the discovery service.

`@grafana/plugin-compat` (currently 0.12.0) already does this for `getPluginSettings`, `updateAppPluginSettings`, `getAppPluginHealth`, `callAppPluginProxy` (`src/apps.ts`) and `callDataSourcePluginProxy` (`src/datasources.ts`). Its wrappers forward to stable `@grafana/runtime` exports (`typeof fn === 'function'`) and fall back otherwise. It can't import `@grafana/runtime/unstable` (#137185), which is why the service is exported from the stable entry point.

Add a new entry point, `@grafana/plugin-compat/apis`, exporting `getApiGroup`, `resolveApiVersion` and `resolveApiBaseURL` right after #137724, and `isApiResourceAvailable` after #138734.

| Grafana version the plugin runs on | Compat does | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Has the runtime export | Forwards to it | Shared cache, invalidated on plugin installs |
| No export, serves `/apis` | Its own `GET /apis/<group>/` (and `/apis/<group>/<version>` for resources), sharing in-flight requests | Correct answers, no shared cache or invalidation |
| `/apis` fails, `404`, no session | `undefined` / `false` | The plugin uses its legacy path, which is right: the new APIs aren't there either |

- The fallback never throws.
- The fallback resolves versions with the same rule as the runtime (preferred if listed, else most stable shared, else `undefined`), pinned by the same test cases.
- Document the pattern for plugin teams: resolve the base URL, call it with your own client, fall back to legacy when it's `undefined`. This was requested in [#proj-mt-plugins](https://grafanalabs.enterprise.slack.com/archives/C097U3KEY9H/p1793874019374839?thread_ts=1793872463.197529&cid=C097U3KEY9H).

API clients: Resolve generated client base URLs through discovery

**Parent:** #137723 · **Depends on:** #137724

The generator writes a fixed URL into every generated RTK client (`renderBaseAPI` in `packages/grafana-api-clients/src/generator/templates.ts`):

```
baseQuery: createBaseQuery({ baseURL: BASE_URL }),
```

When the backend promotes a group, every client needs a code change. Only the folder client resolves its version at runtime, through a hand-written resolver (`folder/v1beta1/folderApiVersionResolver.ts`). `createBaseQuery` already supports an async `getBaseURL`.

```
 export const API_VERSION = 'v1' as const;
+export const COMPATIBLE_VERSIONS = [API_VERSION] as const;
 export const BASE_URL = getAPIBaseURL(API_GROUP, API_VERSION);
 ...
-  baseQuery: createBaseQuery({ baseURL: BASE_URL }),
+  baseQuery: createBaseQuery({
+    getBaseURL: async () => (await resolveApiBaseURL(API_GROUP, COMPATIBLE_VERSIONS)) ?? BASE_URL,
+  }),
```

- `COMPATIBLE_VERSIONS` defaults to the generated version. Extra versions with the same schema come from the client's entry in `createAPIConfig(...)`: `src/scripts/generate-rtk-apis.ts` (OSS) and `local/generate-enterprise-apis.ts` (Enterprise). Compatibility is a human decision. The generator can diff the OpenAPI documents to warn.
- Falling back to `BASE_URL` keeps today's behavior, so the change is safe for every client.
- `@grafana/api-clients` declares a peer dependency of `@grafana/runtime >=11.6`. The generated code has to fall back to `BASE_URL` when the runtime doesn't have `resolveApiBaseURL`.
- Cluster-scoped groups pass `{ namespaced: false }`.
- Replace the folder resolver with `COMPATIBLE_VERSIONS = ['v1beta1', 'v1']`.
- Regenerate all `baseAPI.ts` files in a separate PR, so the generator change stays readable. Check the hand-written ones (e.g. `preferences/{org,user,team}/baseAPI.ts`) separately.

Runtime: Resolve plugin settings, health and proxy API versions through discovery

**Parent:** #137723 · **Depends on:** #137724

The plugin wrappers in `@grafana/runtime` build `/apis` URLs from `getApiVersion()` (`services/pluginUtils.ts`), which always returns `'v0alpha1'`. It's already async (#137597), so callers await it:

- `getPluginSettings`, `refetchPluginSettings`, `updateAppPluginSettings` (`services/pluginSettings/`)
- `getAppPluginHealth` (`services/pluginHealth/getAppPluginHealth.ts`)
- `callAppPluginProxy` (`services/pluginProxy/callAppPluginProxy.ts`, #137300)
- `callDataSourcePluginProxy` (`services/pluginProxy/callDataSourcePluginProxy.ts`, #137926)

Both proxy wrappers accept an explicit `apiVersion` (validated by `assertApiVersion`, #137457) and default to `getApiVersion()`.

Whether the MT path is used depends on `plugins.useMTPluginSettings` and a plugin meta cache hit, not on whether the server serves the plugin's group.

- Replace `getApiVersion()` with `resolveApiBaseURL(<plugin group>, SUPPORTED_VERSIONS)` in each wrapper.
- If the group isn't served, or discovery is unknown, use the existing legacy path (`/api/plugins/<id>/settings`, `/api/plugin-proxy/<id>/…`, `/api/datasources/proxy/uid/<uid>/…`) instead of failing.
- Keep the feature flag as the rollout gate. Discovery only answers whether the API is there and in which version.
- Keep the explicit `apiVersion` argument of the proxy wrappers as an override.
- Note: `app/instance/proxy` and `health` aren't listed in discovery (they're HTTP middleware, not registered subresources). Only check the group, not the subresource.

The `plugins.grafana.app` metas (`services/pluginMeta/`) are a separate sub-issue: they load on the boot path, so resolving their version adds a request in series there.

**Parent:** #137723 · **Depends on:** #137724

The API discovery cache lives for the whole page load. When a plugin is installed, updated, uninstalled, enabled or disabled, the set of `/apis` groups (or their versions) changes, but the cache keeps the old answer. A just-installed app plugin then looks "not available" until the user reloads the page.

On self-hosted Grafana it doesn't reload at all: #136473 (merged) adds plugin store events, but `PluginLoader.Notify` doesn't subscribe to them yet. Callers should treat "absent right after install" as normal. Optionally, the catalog retries discovery once after a delay.

Runtime: Add an API discovery service

**Parent:** #137723

The frontend has no shared way to ask the server which `/apis` groups and versions it serves. Every feature that needs to know runs its own discovery: dashboards, folders, alert rules, annotations, library panels, provisioning, Live, the data source settings save and the query library. `@grafana/runtime` and plugins can't import any of them, because the helpers in `public/app/features/apiserver/discovery.ts` are internal to the app.

Add a discovery service to `@grafana/runtime` (`packages/grafana-runtime/src/services/apiDiscovery/`), exported from the stable `@grafana/runtime` entry point and tagged `@alpha` until the API settles. It reports what the server serves and builds base URLs. It doesn't make requests or choose legacy fallbacks.

This issue covers the **group level**. Resource-level lookups (`getApiResources`, `isApiResourceAvailable`, `getAllApiResources`) are a separate follow-up, because none of the first consumers need them.

```
getApiGroup(group): Promise<ApiGroupInfo | undefined>; // { group, versions, preferredVersion }
resolveApiVersion(group, supported: readonly string[]): Promise<string | undefined>;
resolveApiBaseURL(group, supported: readonly string[], opts?: { namespaced?: boolean }): Promise<string | undefined>;
invalidateApiDiscovery(): void;
```

**Fetching**

- Groups come from plain `GET /apis` (`APIGroupList`). If the root request fails, fall back to `GET /apis/<group>/`. Behind the router this has happened before: #136138, #136201.
- Concurrent callers share one in-flight request.
- Discovery never blocks first paint and never runs without a signed-in session (#135848, #135876). Reuse `isSignedInAnonymousOrPublicAccess()`, as the data source cache does.
- A timeout of a few seconds counts as "unknown".

**Version resolution**

`resolveApiVersion` returns the server's preferred version if the caller lists it. Otherwise it returns the most stable version both sides have (`v1` > `v1beta1` > `v1alpha1` > `v0alpha1`), otherwise `undefined`. It never returns a version the caller didn't list.

**Outcomes**

| Outcome | Caller sees | Cached? |
|---|---|---|
| Served | `ApiGroupInfo` / version / URL | Until `invalidateApiDiscovery()` or reload |
| Not served (`404` / absent) | `undefined` | Until `invalidateApiDiscovery()` or reload |
| Unknown (error, timeout, `401`) | `undefined` | No; the next caller retries |

**Tests and observability**

- A test helper (e.g. `setApiDiscoveryForTesting()`) and MSW handlers in `@grafana/test-utils` for `/apis` and `/apis/<group>/`.
- One log event per failed or timed-out discovery request, not one per caller.
- No error toasts.

> [!NOTE]
> Measure the size of plain vs. aggregated `/apis` on a stack with many plugins, and check what a Viewer gets in MT. The results may change the fetch strategy, but not the API.

- Stable export, not `unstable`: `@grafana/plugin-compat` can't import `@grafana/runtime/unstable` (plugins failed to load on Grafana older than 11.6, see #137185), so it can only forward to stable exports. Plugins use the service through compat (#137731), so the `@alpha` API can still change; compat absorbs it.

Runtime: Resolve API availability and versions through API discovery

**Parent:** #114536

**Frontend code that calls `/apis` hardcodes the API group and version, and assumes the API is there. The server is never asked.**

- [`getApiVersion()`](https://github.com/grafana/grafana/blob/main/packages/grafana-runtime/src/services/pluginUtils.ts#L3) always returns `v0alpha1`
  - used by plugin settings, plugin metas, app plugin health, `callAppPluginProxy` and `callDataSourcePluginProxy`

  - library panels
  - provisioning

  - query library

**A discovery service in `@grafana/runtime`**, exported from the stable `@grafana/runtime` entry point and tagged `@alpha` until the API settles.
